food_cultures.summary_en: A Toshima product-development project uses yeast isolated from camellia flowers to explore a distinctive island beer. The initiative is intended to create another use for the village's central agricultural resource.

facts.claim_en: Tokyo's official islands initiative describes trials using camellia flower yeast, with camellia oil also under consideration for the recipe.

food_cultures.summary_en: This pale-skinned heritage sweet potato was a vital food crop on Niijima's sandy, rice-unsuitable land. It remains central to local cooking, sweets and shochu, including foods made with potatoes grown on Shikinejima.

facts.claim_en: The local agricultural cooperative documents the crop's role as a historical staple and its identity as the Shichifuku sweet-potato variety.
The village tourism site identifies America-imo as a traditional potato used for roasting, sweets, dumplings and shochu.

places.relation_en: Local cooperative selling island-grown vegetables and America-imo processed foods.

makers.relation_en: Supports production and sells local crops and processed foods.

food_cultures.notes_en: A foundational ingredient connecting several otherwise distinct Niijima and Shikinejima food cultures.

food_cultures.summary_en: A traditional island preparation in which small America-imo sweet potatoes are boiled in seawater. The practice is remembered as part of everyday life and childhood outings by the shore.

facts.claim_en: JA Niijima describes gutsuni as an old preparation of small America-imo cooked in seawater.

food_cultures.notes_en: Historical household dish; no contemporary commercial serving location was verified.

food_cultures.summary_en: Traditional dumplings prepared from the local sweet potato. The cooperative describes versions that may be fried, steamed or cooked in soup.

facts.claim_en: JA Niijima identifies imo dango as a regional dish and sells a prepared base made with America-imo and starch.

places.relation_en: Cooperative associated with the America-imo dumpling base.

makers.relation_en: Produces or distributes the documented dumpling base.

food_cultures.summary_en: Ashitaba is a common island vegetable eaten in tempura, seasoned greens, stir-fries and rice. It also supplies flavor to many local snacks and processed foods.

facts.claim_en: JA Niijima documents ashitaba cultivation, cooking methods and harvest timing.

places.relation_en: Local source for vegetables and ashitaba-based processed foods.

makers.relation_en: Local agricultural cooperative.

food_cultures.season_en: Harvested year-round, with spring and autumn peaks

food_cultures.summary_en: Niijima's small rakkyo bulbs are harvested young for their sweetness and tenderness. They are eaten fresh with miso, pickled or cooked.

facts.claim_en: The agricultural cooperative identifies early harvesting and the characteristic sweetness of Niijima rakkyo.

places.relation_en: Local agricultural sales point.

makers.relation_en: Handles locally grown island rakkyo.

food_cultures.summary_en: Onions grown in Niijima's sandy soil and strong seasonal winds are known for their sweetness, allowing them to be enjoyed raw as well as cooked.

facts.claim_en: JA Niijima describes the influence of the island's sandy soil and winter winds on its sweet onion crop.

places.relation_en: Producer cooperative and local vegetable outlet.

food_cultures.notes_en: The village also identifies the onions as an agricultural branding effort.

food_cultures.summary_en: A locally grown chili valued for pronounced heat and aroma. Green chilies are commonly used with sashimi, while red chilies appear in seasonings and preserves.

facts.claim_en: The agricultural cooperative describes local red and green chilies and the use of green chili as a sashimi condiment.

places.relation_en: Carries local chili-based seasonings.

food_cultures.summary_en: Jinenjo is a traditional yam eaten on Niijima, including raw, grated or fried preparations.

facts.claim_en: The village tourism site identifies jinenjo as a local mountain food and describes its customary preparation.

food_cultures.notes_en: The source does not establish a specific public foraging location.

food_cultures.name_ja: ふきんとう・ツワブキ
food_cultures.summary_en: Known locally as fukinto, the young stalks of tsuwabuki are a traditional island vegetable. They are prepared in soy-based pickles, miso preserves and stir-fries.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies fukinto as the local name for tsuwabuki and documents ways its tender shoots are eaten.

food_cultures.summary_en: Akaika is one of Niijima and Shikinejima's signature seafood catches. The squid is eaten fresh, simmered, dried and used in a locally developed yakisoba dish.

facts.claim_en: Niijima Village identifies spring-to-early-summer red squid as a major local ingredient.

food_cultures.notes_en: The local brand page identifies akaika with kensaki squid.

food_cultures.summary_en: Red squid caught around Shikinejima is simmered in a sweet-savory seasoning, creating a recognized regional seafood dish.

facts.claim_en: The Niijima-Shikinejima certified-brand registry identifies simmered Shikinejima red squid as a local dish.

makers.relation_en: Producer of the recognized simmered red squid.

food_cultures.summary_en: A locally recognized seafood product made by drying red squid to concentrate its flavor.

facts.claim_en: The certified-brand registry lists overnight-dried red squid as a Shikinejima processed seafood product.

makers.name_ja: 式根島おさかなサービス
makers.relation_en: Maker of overnight-dried red squid.

food_cultures.summary_en: A branded line of Niijima red squid caught by local fishermen and processed into dried seafood. Its products include more extensively dried squid, snack-style pieces and overnight-dried versions.

facts.claim_en: The certified-brand registry describes the squid's local catch, drying process and three product styles.

makers.relation_en: Local fishing and seafood-processing producer behind the Ika Yaro line.

food_cultures.summary_en: A modern Niijima and Shikinejima regional noodle dish combining local red squid, thick noodles and a sweet-savory sauce.

facts.claim_en: The Niijima Village Chamber of Commerce identifies akaika yakisoba as a signature regional dish made with locally caught squid.

places.relation_en: Shikinejima food shop associated with local dishes including red-squid yakisoba.

food_cultures.notes_en: Different establishments may prepare their own versions.

food_cultures.name_ja: 青ムロアジ・ムロアジ漁
food_cultures.summary_en: Muroaji is an important fish in Niijima's food economy, supplying the preserved fish used for kusaya and the minced fish used in tataki.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies local blue muroaji as a fish used in Niijima kusaya production.
The village's gourmet guide describes muroaji as the basis of traditional tataki fish paste.

food_cultures.season_en: Locally caught blue muroaji used for kusaya is identified for August–November.

food_cultures.summary_en: A traditional seasoned fish paste made from locally caught muroaji, sometimes with flying fish. It can be fried into fish cakes or added to soups and hot pots.

facts.claim_en: The village describes tataki as seasoned minced fish combined with ingredients such as ginger and onion.
The certified-brand registry documents both Niijima and Shikinejima producers of tataki.

makers.relation_en: Producer of certified Niijima tataki.

makers.name_ja: にいじま漁業協同組合 式根島事業所
makers.relation_en: Produces a Shikinejima version using muroaji and flying fish.

food_cultures.notes_en: The regional meaning is seasoned fish paste, not the seared meat preparation also called tataki elsewhere in Japan.

food_cultures.summary_en: Niijima is particularly associated with kusaya, fish soaked in inherited fermented brine and dried. Producers use different local fish and maintain their own distinctive brines.

facts.claim_en: Niijima Village describes the traditional brine and the different fish species used in kusaya production.
The Chamber of Commerce identifies Niijima kusaya as a local specialty with more than three centuries of history.

places.relation_en: Island seafood-processing district associated with the local kusaya cooperative.

makers.name_ja: 新島水産加工業協同組合

food_cultures.season_en: Different fish are processed across the year.
food_cultures.notes_en: Do not confuse Niijima's producer network with the separate kusaya makers on Oshima.

food_cultures.summary_en: A processed form of Niijima kusaya that has already been grilled and portioned, offering another way to enjoy the island's fermented-fish tradition.

facts.claim_en: The Chamber of Commerce lists prepared grilled kusaya as a certified Niijima product.

places.relation_en: Island processing district associated with the producers.

food_cultures.summary_en: A Shikinejima pasta dish combining Niijima kusaya, island nori and chili-infused oil in a locally inspired variation of aglio e olio.

facts.claim_en: The regional certified-brand registry identifies a kusaya-and-seaweed spaghetti by Miyatora.

food_cultures.summary_en: A burger built around a fried local-fish patty mixed with Shikinejima ashitaba. It is a modern adaptation of traditional island tataki.

food_cultures.summary_en: A seafood rice bowl featuring locally landed fish marinated in a special soy-based sauce and served over vinegared rice.

facts.claim_en: The certified-brand registry describes a bowl prepared with seasonal Shikinejima fish including medai and kanpachi.

makers.relation_en: Producer associated with the certified island-marinated seafood bowl.

food_cultures.summary_en: Rice balls that bring together Shikinejima ashitaba preserves and naturally gathered rock laver.

facts.claim_en: The Chamber of Commerce certified-brand listing identifies island rice balls made with locally grown ashitaba and natural rock laver.

places.relation_en: Maker of the certified island rice balls.

makers.relation_en: Producer of island rice balls.

food_cultures.summary_en: A Shikinejima pasta preparation using homegrown ashitaba, onions, garlic and island chili peppers.

facts.claim_en: The certified-brand registry describes Ikemura Shoten's ashitaba pasta made with island-grown vegetables.

places.relation_en: Producer associated with the local ashitaba pasta.

makers.relation_en: Maker of the certified pasta dish.

food_cultures.summary_en: Spiny lobster from the waters around the village is an established high-value catch, used in sashimi, grilled dishes and soups.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies spiny lobster as a valued local marine food and ceremonial gift.

food_cultures.notes_en: This is a fishing and food tradition, not a suggestion that visitors collect shellfish or lobster themselves.

food_cultures.summary_en: Kinmedai caught in waters around the Izu Islands is a prominent local fish, especially valued in simmered preparations.

facts.claim_en: The Niijima tourism guide describes the area's kinmedai catch and its use in simmered dishes.

food_cultures.season_en: Winter is highlighted as its best season.

food_cultures.summary_en: Takabe is a locally enjoyed summer fish, commonly grilled with salt or simmered.

facts.claim_en: The municipality identifies takabe as a representative summer fish and describes its local cooking methods.

food_cultures.summary_en: Turban shell is part of Niijima's local shellfish cuisine, including grilled and simmered dishes.

facts.claim_en: The Niijima tourism guide includes sazae among the village's characteristic local shellfish.

food_cultures.summary_en: Tokobushi is another locally caught shellfish that appears in the village's seafood cooking.

facts.claim_en: The Niijima tourism guide identifies tokobushi among the shellfish found around the islands.

food_cultures.summary_en: Kamenote, a shellfish-like marine invertebrate named for its resemblance to a turtle's foot, is counted among the village's edible coastal resources.

facts.claim_en: The municipality includes kamenote among the local marine foods collected around Niijima.

food_cultures.notes_en: No independent coastal collecting activity is suggested.

food_cultures.summary_en: Wild rock laver gathered from island coasts is an established local food, used in rice dishes, noodles and processed specialty foods.

facts.claim_en: Niijima Village lists rock laver among its characteristic food souvenirs.
The certified-brand registry identifies natural rock laver as an ingredient in Shikinejima rice balls and kusaya spaghetti.

food_cultures.summary_en: Milk crackers are also an established Niijima confection, appearing among the municipality's signature food souvenirs.

facts.claim_en: The village identifies milk crackers among Niijima and Shikinejima specialty products.
The local brand registry identifies milk crackers as the base for a separate ashitaba-flavored confection.

makers.relation_en: Maker of a certified milk-cracker-based ashitaba confection.

food_cultures.notes_en: Distinct local production context from Oshima's better-documented milk-cracker history.

food_cultures.summary_en: A Niijima confection incorporating locally grown ashitaba paste into the island's milk-cracker tradition.

makers.relation_en: Producer of certified ashitaba milk crackers.

makers.relation_en: Maker of the certified ashitaba chiffon cake.

makers.relation_en: Baker of the certified pound cake.

facts.claim_en: The local certified-brand registry identifies an America-imo pound cake combining Shikinejima potatoes and Jinata shochu.

makers.relation_en: Maker of the America-imo pound cake.

food_cultures.summary_en: A small butter cake made with farm-grown Niijima ashitaba, representing a modern confection created from island agricultural produce.

facts.claim_en: The Chamber of Commerce lists ashitaba financiers as a certified product made with locally cultivated ashitaba.

makers.relation_en: Farm producer of the certified ashitaba confection.

food_cultures.summary_en: Short, crumbly cookies made using Niijima ashitaba, another example of the local green's use in confectionery.

facts.claim_en: The certified-brand registry lists ashitaba sable cookies made from island-grown ashitaba.

makers.relation_en: Maker of the certified cookies.

food_cultures.summary_en: A smooth sweet-potato cream made with Shikinejima-grown America-imo, preserving the crop's sweetness in a modern spread.

facts.claim_en: The regional certified-brand registry identifies a Shikinejima America-imo cream product.

makers.relation_en: Maker of the certified sweet-potato cream.

food_cultures.summary_en: A preserve combining Niijima's heritage white sweet potato with apple, offered as a local agricultural specialty.

facts.claim_en: JA Niijima lists jam made from the locally distinctive pale-skinned sweet potato and apple.
A-FARM's America-imo jam also appears in the regional certified-brand registry.

food_cultures.summary_en: Young, tender Niijima rakkyo bulbs are preserved in salt, turning the local spring crop into a recognized regional product.

places.relation_en: Producer cooperative associated with the certified preserved rakkyo.

makers.relation_en: Producer of the certified preserved rakkyo.

food_cultures.name_en: Fresh and Dried Island Chili Condiments
food_cultures.summary_en: Niijima's pungent green and red chilies are processed into fresh chopped condiments and dried chili seasonings, maintaining their traditional association with sashimi and everyday cooking.

facts.claim_en: JA Niijima lists fresh island chili, green-chili seasoning and red-chili seasoning among its processed foods.

food_cultures.summary_en: A seasoned miso paste using the island's aromatic green chili peppers, commonly paired with rice or other foods.

facts.claim_en: The Chamber of Commerce identifies chili miso made with summer-harvested green chili as a certified regional product.

makers.relation_en: Maker of a certified chili miso.
